text: According to the passage, why do companies adopt sectional cutoffs?
options: They are cheap to apply and easy to defend|They measure the skills every role needs|They are required by most recruitment rules|They reduce the number of applications received
explanation: The first paragraph says companies adopt them because they are cheap to apply and easy to defend: one number per section against one threshold, with no judgement to explain. The passage does not claim they measure what every role needs -- the second paragraph argues the opposite.
passage:
A sectional cutoff is a promise that a candidate who is strong overall but weak in one area will be set aside. Companies adopt them because they are cheap to apply and easy to defend: a single number per section, compared against a single threshold, with no judgement to explain. The cost is paid by a particular kind of candidate -- the one whose weakest section is the one the job needs least -- and that cost is invisible in the aggregate, because nobody counts the people a filter removed.

The defensible version of a cutoff states what it is for. If a role genuinely requires arithmetic under time pressure, a numerical cutoff measures something the work will demand. If it does not, the cutoff is measuring only the candidate's practice with a particular kind of question, and a college preparing students for it is teaching them to pass a filter rather than to do a job. Both may be worth doing; they are not the same thing, and a placement cell that cannot say which it is doing cannot improve either.

text: Whose cost does the passage say is invisible in the aggregate?
options: The candidate whose weakest section is the one the job needs least|The company that applies the cutoff|The candidate who fails every section|The placement cell that sets the threshold

text: Why does the passage say a mock test is not a forecast?
options: It is a sample of one, taken under conditions the student chose|Its questions are easier than the real paper's|It is marked by a machine rather than a person|Its score is never recorded accurately
explanation: The first paragraph gives that reason in those words: a sample of one, taken under conditions the student chose, usually at home and usually when they felt ready. Nothing is claimed about the difficulty or the marking.
passage:
A mock test tells a student where they stand against the paper they just sat. It is tempting to read it as a forecast of the real one, and the temptation grows with every mock that turns out to have been roughly right. But a mock is a sample of one, taken under conditions the student chose, usually at home and usually when they felt ready.

What a mock does well is narrow attention. A report that names the three weakest topics is worth more than a score, because it says what to do next. A score says only how today went, and a single score repeated over weeks says less than the direction those scores move in. The students who improve fastest are generally the ones who treat each report as a list of topics rather than as a verdict.
passageTitle: Why a mock test is not a prediction

text: What distinction does the passage draw between two kinds of practice?
options: Practising a method against practising the recognition of which method applies|Practising alone against practising in a group|Practising with a timer against practising without one|Practising easy questions against practising unfamiliar ones
explanation: The passage contrasts practising a method -- working carefully through a hard question teaches the method it uses -- with practising the recognition of which method applies, which is what working quickly through many easier ones teaches. Timers and company are not the distinction.
passage:
There is a difference between practising a problem and practising the recognition of problems. Working carefully through a hard question teaches the method it uses. Working quickly through forty easier ones teaches which method a question is asking for, which is a separate skill and the one a timed paper rewards.

Most students do one of the two and assume it covers both. Those who only do hard problems find that they know what to do but run out of time; those who only do easy ones find that they recognise everything and can finish nothing unfamiliar. The useful week contains some of each, and the useful report tells a student which of the two they have been neglecting.

text: According to the passage, what happens to a student who only works through hard problems?
options: They know what to do but run out of time|They recognise everything and finish nothing unfamiliar|They lose interest in the easier topics|They score well on every timed paper
explanation: The second paragraph says those who only do hard problems find that they know what to do but run out of time. The second option is what it says about the opposite habit, which is why it is the distractor.
